chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Case for Multi-Asset Systematic Investing

lessons.title: Why Single-Asset Strategies Break: Concentration, Regime Risk, and Correlation Spikes

body.text: A portfolio of fifty NSE stocks across ten sectors is not diversified if every one of those fifty stocks gets hit by the same macro shock at the same time. Diversification is not a function of how many tickers you hold. It is a function of how many genuinely independent sources of return sit inside your book, and one asset class, however finely sliced, is still one source.

children.text: Most traders who call their equity book "diversified" mean something narrower than they think. A basket of Nifty 50 constituents spread across banking, IT, FMCG, and pharma looks spread out on a stock screener like screener.in. It is still a single bet on Indian equities as an asset class, and in a systemic shock, sector labels stop mattering. This lesson is about why that matters, and why a systematic book built on one asset class, however well constructed within that asset class, carries a structural weakness that no amount of stock selection or sector rotation can fix.
The Concentration Problem Hiding in a "Diversified" Equity Portfolio

Picture a prop desk running a systematic long-only momentum equity book: thirty NSE names, sector-diversified, rebalanced monthly. On paper this looks well spread out. Through most of 2019, it behaved that way too, with idiosyncratic stock moves mostly cancelling out and the book's day-to-day volatility running below that of any single name in it. Then came March 2020. In about four weeks, the Nifty 50 fell close to 38% peak to trough, and it did not fall because IT stocks and banking stocks had thirty separate, unrelated bad months. It fell because every sector sold off together, as global risk appetite collapsed and foreign portfolio investors pulled capital out of Indian equities almost indiscriminately.

children.text: Same Story With a Single Systematic Strategy, Not Just a Single Stock Book

This holds even when a desk blends multiple equity strategies rather than running just one. A book that combines a momentum sleeve, a low-volatility sleeve, and a quality-factor sleeve, all trading NSE equities, can show genuinely low correlation between those sleeves in normal markets. Each factor responds to a different driver day to day. But all three sleeves still share the same dominant risk factor underneath: broad Indian equity market beta. Diversifying which stocks or which factors you hold reduces single-name and single-factor risk. It does nothing for the risk that the entire asset class moves together on the same bad day.

body.text: Low correlation between strategies inside one asset class is not the same thing as diversification. It protects you from a factor-specific drawdown. It offers close to nothing on the day the whole asset class sells off together.

children.text: What Real Diversification Requires: Assets That Don't Share a Regime

Genuine diversification needs a second, or third, source of return that is not simply a repackaging of the same underlying risk factor. Equities are driven primarily by corporate earnings growth and risk appetite. Government bonds, G-Secs, are driven by interest rate expectations and, often, by exactly the kind of risk-off flows that hurt equities. Gold has historically behaved as a store of value during periods of currency and equity market stress. The Indian rupee's moves against the US dollar carry their own drivers, tied to capital flows, the current account, and RBI policy. None of these are perfectly independent of each other, but they are not the same bet wearing different tickers either, which is exactly what a book built entirely from NSE and BSE equities is.

children.text: Take a book that is 60% Nifty 50 equities, with annualized volatility of roughly 20%, and 40% gold, with annualized volatility of roughly 12%. In a calm regime where the correlation between the two runs close to 0.1, the formula above gives a portfolio volatility of around 13%, noticeably below the 16.8% you would get by simply weighting the two volatilities together with no diversification credit at all. In a stress regime where that correlation rises to 0.7, the same formula gives a portfolio volatility of around 16%, most of the diversification benefit gone even though the position sizes never changed.

children.text: Correlation Spikes Are a Feature of Crises, Not a Bug in Your Data

markDefs.definition: The tendency for asset correlations that were low in calm markets to rise sharply together during a systemic crisis, as investors stop distinguishing between individual holdings and simply sell risk assets to raise cash or move to safety.

children.text: This is not a modeling quirk. It is a well-documented feature of how systemic crises actually unfold. When a shock is large and broad enough, whether it is a global pandemic, a banking crisis, or a sudden capital flight from emerging markets including India, investors stop asking which specific asset they are holding and start asking one question: is this safe, or is this risk? Everything on the risk side of that line, NSE large-caps, BSE mid-caps, corporate bonds, tends to get sold together. Everything on the safe side, sovereign G-Secs, gold on MCX, sometimes the US dollar against the rupee, tends to get bought together. This is exactly what a
is, and it is why India VIX and cross-asset correlation both tend to rise together in a genuine panic.

body.text: Diversification's entire job is to earn you a smoother ride in calm markets and a cushion in stress. A book built from one asset class can only ever do the first half of that job. It has nothing else to lean on the one day the whole asset class moves together.

body.title: The Systematic Desk That Was "Diversified" on Paper
body.scenario: A small systematic desk in Mumbai runs three equity strategies on NSE stocks: a momentum book, a low-volatility book, and a quality-factor book, each rebalanced monthly and each individually backtested to a healthy Sharpe ratio above 1.2 over 2015 to 2019. The desk head describes the combined book as well diversified because the three factor sleeves have historically shown low correlation to each other. In March 2020, all three sleeves lost between 24% and 31% in the same four weeks, and the combined book's drawdown was barely better than holding the Nifty 50 outright.
body.prompt: Was the desk head's diversification claim wrong, and if so, where exactly did the diversification logic break down?
body.modelAnswer: The claim was not wrong about factor correlation in normal markets. Momentum, low-volatility, and quality factors genuinely can behave differently from each other most of the time. It was wrong about what kind of diversification that provides. All three sleeves are still equity-only strategies, so all three share the same dominant risk factor: broad Indian equity market beta. Low correlation between factors inside one asset class protects against factor-specific drawdowns, not against a systemic shock that hits the asset class itself. To actually reduce the March 2020 drawdown, the desk needed exposure to a different asset class entirely, such as G-Secs or gold, that does not share equities' dominant risk driver.

body.title: Computing Portfolio Volatility Under Stress Correlation
body.prompt: A book holds 60% in Nifty 50 equities (annualized volatility 20%) and 40% in gold (annualized volatility 12%). Using the two-asset portfolio volatility formula, what is the portfolio's annualized volatility (%) if the correlation between equities and gold rises to 0.7 in a stress regime? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: sigma_p^2 = (0.6^2 x 20^2) + (0.4^2 x 12^2) + (2 x 0.6 x 0.4 x 0.7 x 20 x 12) = 144 + 23.04 + 80.64 = 247.68. The square root of 247.68 is approximately 15.7%, which rounds to 16%. Compare this to the calm-regime figure of about 13% from earlier in the lesson. The entire difference comes from the correlation term, not from any change in position size.

body.title: Naming the Failure Mode
body.textWithBlank: The tendency for asset correlations that were low in calm markets to rise sharply together during a systemic crisis, eroding diversification exactly when it is needed most, is known as a ___.
body.explanation: All three phrases describe the same phenomenon: diversification benefits shrinking or disappearing during stress because previously unrelated or low-correlated assets start moving together. Measuring this directly, and building portfolios that survive it, is the central task starting from Chapter 3 of this course.

points: Spreading a book across many NSE stocks reduces single-name risk, but it does not reduce exposure to the equity market itself moving as one
A sector-diversified or even factor-diversified equity book still carries one dominant risk driver: broad equity market beta
In the March 2020 crash, pairwise correlations across Indian equities rose sharply as nearly every sector and factor sleeve sold off together
Genuine diversification requires assets with different underlying drivers, such as equities, G-Secs, gold, and currencies, not just different tickers within one asset class
Portfolio volatility depends heavily on the correlation between assets, and that correlation is not fixed, it can move sharply between calm and stress regimes
Correlation spikes during crises are a well-documented feature of how systemic shocks unfold, not a modeling artifact, which is why this course is built around multiple asset classes rather than one
